lead: On the Monday of the first week after Pentecost the Epistle shows the Church as God's house, built of living people on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ as the cornerstone, “a dwelling place for God”. The Gospel is the sad close of Jesus' public ministry in John: many signs, little faith, and some who believed but were afraid to say so, “for they loved human glory more than the glory that comes from God.” The key words are household and glory.

r.h: No longer strangers: a dwelling place for God
set: Ephesians is above all a letter about the Church. The letter names Paul as its author, and the Church's tradition received it as his; many scholars today think it was written by a disciple of Paul in his name, late in the first century. Either way the Church reads it as inspired Scripture.

Just before today's verses the writer reminds the Gentile believers that they were once “far off”, without hope, and that Christ “has broken down the dividing wall” to make Jew and Gentile one in himself (2:13–14). The Gentiles are joined to the promises God made to Israel, not set in Israel's place. Today's verses draw the conclusion with the picture of a building.
str: v. 19: no longer strangers: citizens and members of God's household.
v. 20: the foundation of apostles and prophets; Christ the cornerstone.
vv. 21–22: the building grows into a holy temple, a dwelling place for God in the Spirit.
kw: Two kinds of outsider: the foreigner passing through, and the resident alien who lived in a place without a citizen's rights. Now the Gentile believers are “citizens with the saints” and members of God's own family.

The stone that holds the building together and fixes its lines. The image comes from Isaiah 28:16, “a precious cornerstone”, and Psalm 118:22, “the stone that the builders rejected”. Some scholars think it may mean the top stone that completes the arch. Either way, the whole building depends on Christ.
vv: So then you are no longer strangers and aliens, but you are citizens with the saints and also members of the household of God,
From outsiders to family. In the Church no one is a guest on sufferance. Every baptized person belongs to the household.
in whom you also are built together spiritually into a dwelling place for God.
The Greek says “in the Spirit”. The temple of stone in Jerusalem was the place of God's presence; now the Spirit makes a people into his dwelling.
ch: The Catechism gathers the Bible's images of the Church as a building: the house of God in which his family dwells, built on the apostles, with Christ as the cornerstone (CCC 756). It teaches that the Church is the temple of the Holy Spirit, who is to the Body of Christ what the soul is to the human body (CCC 797–798). In a parish this means that the living stones matter more than the walls, and that no one should feel a stranger there.

r.h: They loved human glory more than the glory of God
set: These verses close the first half of John's Gospel, often called the Book of Signs (chapters 1–12). Jesus has worked his great signs, the last of them the raising of Lazarus (chapter 11). He has entered Jerusalem and spoken of the grain of wheat that must die to bear fruit (12:24). Now John steps back and asks why so many did not believe, and he answers with two passages of Isaiah.

Jesus, his mother and all the first disciples were Jews. When John speaks of opposition, he usually means the religious authorities in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people as such. In today's passage John himself says that many, even of the authorities, believed in him.
str: v. 37: many signs, yet they did not believe.
vv. 42–43: believers who would not confess, for fear and for love of human glory.
kw: John's word for Jesus' miracles: deeds that point beyond themselves to who he is. Signs invite faith; they do not force it.

The same word is used in v. 41 of the glory Isaiah saw and in v. 43 of “human glory”, meaning praise or reputation. John sets the two side by side: the glory of God shown in Jesus, and the small glory of what others think of us.

A word found only in John (9:22; 12:42; 16:2). Many scholars think it reflects the painful separation between synagogue and Church later in the first century, as well as tensions already present in Jesus' lifetime.
vv: Although he had performed so many signs in their presence, they did not believe in him.
An honest admission. Even the clearest signs do not compel belief. Faith remains an answer of the heart.
Isaiah said this because he saw his glory and spoke about him.
Isaiah saw the Lord on his throne in the temple (Isaiah 6:1). John says that the glory Isaiah saw was the glory of the Son. The Word was already at work in Israel's history before he became flesh.
for they loved human glory more than the glory that comes from God.
The quiet sin of good people: not hatred of Jesus, but fear of what others will say. John names it so that we may examine ourselves.
ch: The Church does not read Isaiah's words about blinded eyes as God forcing anyone to refuse him. The prophet speaks of the result of a long refusal as if it were God's own act, because nothing happens outside his providence. St Augustine explained that God blinds and hardens not by making anyone evil, but by leaving people to the darkness they have chosen (Tractates on John 53, in substance). The Church also forbids reading this passage as a judgement on the Jewish people: what happened in the Passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today (Nostra Aetate 4; CCC 597). The question John asks is for every reader.

qa: Does verse 39 mean that they could not believe even if they wanted to?

No. The Bible often speaks of God's permission as if it were his direct action. The people John describes had already seen many signs and refused them. Isaiah's words describe how a heart grows hard by refusing light. God “desires everyone to be saved” (1 Timothy 2:4), and no one is predestined to refuse him (CCC 1037).
study: Is there anyone in our parish who might feel like a “stranger”? What could I do this week to make them feel part of the household?
Where do I keep silent about my faith because I fear what others will say?
